equation.name: How long a star's outer layer takes to churn once
equation.formula:
x = log10(M / M_sun)
tau = 10 ^ (c0 - c1 * x - c2 * x * x) * day

c0.name: fit's value at one solar mass (log days)

tau.name: time for the outer layer to turn over

source.text: Wright, N. J., Drake, J. J., Mamajek, E. E. and Henry, G. W. 2011, ApJ 743, 48

explain.curious: Cool stars boil like a pan of soup under their surfaces. The smaller the star, the deeper and slower the boiling: about two weeks for the Sun, months for a small red dwarf.
explain.science: Empirical turnover time fitted so that X-ray activity against spin over turnover time is one relation for all cool stars. Valid for 0.09 to 1.36 solar masses; stars without a convective outer layer have none.

references: Noyes, R. W., Hartmann, L. W., Baliunas, S. L., Duncan, D. K. and Vaughan, A. H. 1984, Rotation, convection, and magnetic activity in lower main-sequence stars, ApJ 279, 763: activity depends on the Rossby number. doi:10.1086/161945

explain.curious: A star's magnetism comes from spin twisting its boiling layer. What matters is how many turns it makes in one boil: fewer than one, and the star is quiet like the Sun; many, and it is wild.

equation.name: How brightly a star shines in X-rays for its spin
equation.formula:
sat = 10 ^ lsat
Rx = if Ro <= Ro_sat then sat else sat * (Ro / Ro_sat) ^ beta

lsat.name: saturated log of the X-ray share

Rx.name: share of the star's light given off as X-rays

source.text: Wright, N. J., Drake, J. J., Mamajek, E. E. and Henry, G. W. 2011, ApJ 743, 48
source.where: eq. 3, the saturated and unsaturated regimes

explain.curious: The Sun gives out less than a millionth of its power as X-rays. A young fast-spinning star gives out a thousandth, and no amount of extra spin pushes it higher: it is saturated.
explain.science: The activity-rotation relation: flat below the saturation Rossby number, a power law above. The Sun's Rossby number 1.8 gives log(L_X/L_bol) = −6.21 against −6.24 observed.

explain.curious: Quiet stars wax and wane in spots over years, like the Sun's eleven-year cycle. Slower spinners have longer cycles.
explain.science: The short-cycle (inactive) branch of the cycle-rotation diagram. Scatter 0.24 dex; the Sun itself sits between the branches, and this relation gives it 6.1 years against the observed 11.

E_ref.source: the reference energy of Vasilyev et al. 2024's superflare rate

params.description: flares above 10³⁴ erg per second, times 10³⁴ erg, per watt of X-rays (from the Sun-like superflare rate)
index of the energy spread dN/dE ∝ E^−α (Shibayama 2013: 2.0; Vasilyev 2024: 1.97 ± 0.30)

references: Vasilyev, V. et al. 2024, Sun-like stars produce superflares roughly once per century, Science: (8.63 ± 0.20)×10⁻³ per year above 10³⁴ erg for 5000 to 6500 K stars with rotation over 20 days; energy spread dN/dE ∝ E^(−1.97 ± 0.30), consistent with the Sun's own flares extrapolated. https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.12265

Shibayama, T. et al. 2013, Superflares on solar-type stars observed with Kepler I, ApJS 209, 5: dN/dE ∝ E^(−2.0) for slow rotators, −2.2 for all G dwarfs; fast rotators flare far more often. https://arxiv.org/abs/1308.1480
atoms.shown: N(>E) = k (L_X / E₀) (E / E₀)^(1−α),  E₀ = 10³⁴ erg

equation.name: How often a star flares at least this hard
equation.formula:
L = max(Lx, 0)
N = k * L / E_ref * (E / E_ref) ^ (1 - alpha)

N.name: flares per second at least this big

source.text: Vasilyev, V. et al. 2024, Sun-like stars produce superflares roughly once per century, Science
source.where: the superflare rate and energy index

explain.curious: Small flares happen all the time and great ones rarely: ten times the energy, a tenth as often. A star like the Sun has a superflare about once a century; a young or red dwarf star, many a year.
explain.science: A power-law spread of flare energies whose rate scales with the star's X-ray luminosity (both are fed by the same magnetic energy). Normalised to Sun-like stars' superflare rate.

params.description: field of a saturated star at Ro = 1 on its fast branch, gauss (Reiners 2022: 2050)
slope of the fast branch (−0.11 ± 0.03)
field at Ro = 1 on the slow branch, gauss (199)
slope of the slow branch (−1.26 ± 0.10)
Rossby number where the branches meet (the X-ray saturation point)

references: Reiners, A., Shulyak, D., Käpylä, P. J. et al. 2022, Magnetism, rotation, and nonthermal emission in cool stars: average magnetic field measurements in 292 M dwarfs, A&A 662, A41: mean surface field ⟨B⟩ = 199 G Ro^(−1.26 ± 0.10) for slow rotators and 2050 G Ro^(−0.11 ± 0.03) for fast (saturated) rotators. https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00342

equation.name: How strong a star's surface magnetism is for its spin
equation.formula: B = (if Ro <= Ro_sat then Bf * Ro ^ sf else Bs * Ro ^ ss) * gauss

Bf.name: fast branch field at Ro = 1, gauss

Bs.name: slow branch field at Ro = 1, gauss

B.name: mean field over the star's surface

source.text: Reiners, A. et al. 2022, A&A 662, A41
source.where: the two branches of mean field against Rossby number

explain.curious: A star's magnetism is stirred by its spin. The Sun's field averages about a hundred gauss over its surface; a young red dwarf spinning in a day carries thousands, enough to hold up huge clouds of gas.
explain.science: Zeeman-broadening measurements of the mean surface field against Rossby number: a steep power law for slow rotators and a nearly flat one once activity saturates. Fitted on M dwarfs; used for every cool star with a churning outer layer (unverified until the paper search returns).

cgs_flux.source: 1 W m⁻² is 1000 erg s⁻¹ cm⁻²

params.description: coronal temperature in MK at unit X-ray surface flux (cgs) (Johnstone and Güdel 2015: 0.11)
index on the X-ray surface flux (0.26)

references: Johnstone, C. P. and Güdel, M. 2015, The coronal temperatures of low-mass main-sequence stars, A&A 578, A129: mean coronal temperature T̄_cor ≈ 0.11 F_X^0.26 MK, F_X the X-ray surface flux in erg s⁻¹ cm⁻². https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00643

equation.name: How hot a star's corona is
equation.formula:
Fx = max(Lx, 0) / (4 * pi * R * R) * cgs_flux
Tc = k * Fx ^ n * MK

cgs_flux.name: one W m⁻² counted in erg s⁻¹ cm⁻²

source.text: Johnstone, C. P. and Güdel, M. 2015, A&A 578, A129
source.where: mean coronal temperature against X-ray surface flux

explain.curious: Above a star's surface the thin gas is far hotter than the surface itself: about two million degrees over the Sun, ten million or more over an active young star.
explain.science: An empirical fit of emission-measure-weighted coronal temperature to X-ray surface flux across low-mass main-sequence stars (unverified until the paper search returns).

params.description: radiative loss of coronal gas per electron and ion pair, W m³ (Rosner, Tucker and Vaiana 1978 near 1 to 2 MK: about 10⁻²² erg cm³ s⁻¹)
mean mass per particle of fully ionised coronal gas, in atomic mass units

references: Rosner, R., Tucker, W. H. and Vaiana, G. S. 1978, Dynamics of the quiescent solar corona, ApJ 220, 643: optically thin radiative loss function of coronal gas, about 10⁻²² erg cm³ s⁻¹ near 1 to 2 million kelvin. doi:10.1086/155949
atoms.shown: n = √(L_X / (Λ 4πR² H)),  H = k T / (μ m_u g)

equation.name: How dense the gas at the foot of a star's corona is
equation.formula:
H = k_B * Tc / (mu * m_u * g)
n = sqrt(max(Lx, 0) / (Lam * 4 * pi * R * R * H))

n.name: particles per cubic metre at the corona's foot

source.text: Rosner, R., Tucker, W. H. and Vaiana, G. S. 1978, ApJ 220, 643
source.where: the radiative loss function of coronal gas

explain.curious: A star's X-rays are the glow of its corona, so how brightly it shines says how much hot gas it holds. Cool gas caught in the field, the prominences, sits in this gas a hundred times denser and colder.
explain.science: The corona taken as one hydrostatic layer of one scale height over the whole star, glowing optically thin: L_X = n² Λ(T) 4πR² H. The loss function is held at one value for 1 to 2 MK, a stand-in for its full temperature dependence.

params.description: closed field's reach for a star with the reference field, stellar radii (the Sun's source surface, 2.5)
reference field, gauss (the Sun's from the surface field block at Ro 1.8)
growth with field: 1/3 for a dipole held off by an even pressure

references: Schatten, K. H., Wilcox, J. M. and Ness, N. F. 1969, A model of interplanetary and coronal magnetic fields, Solar Physics 6, 442: the Sun's field is closed out to a source surface near 2.5 solar radii (later potential-field models keep 2.5). doi:10.1007/BF00146478

Jardine, M. and Collier Cameron, A. 2019, Slingshot prominences: nature's wind gauges, MNRAS 482, 2853: prominences form at and beyond the co-rotation radius when it lies inside the closed corona. https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.09319
atoms.shown: r_c = 2.5 (B / B☉)^(1/3) stellar radii, at least 1

equation.name: How far out a star's field stays closed

B.name: mean field over the star's surface

r0.name: reach for the reference field, stellar radii

rc.name: reach of the closed field, stellar radii

source.text: Schatten, K. H., Wilcox, J. M. and Ness, N. F. 1969, Solar Physics 6, 442
source.where: the source surface at 2.5 solar radii

explain.curious: Near the star its field lines loop back to the surface and can hold gas up; further out the wind drags them open. A stronger field keeps its loops closed further out.
explain.science: The Sun's source surface at 2.5 radii, scaled to other stars as a dipole (falling as r⁻³) balanced against an even outside pressure, which grows as the cube root of the field. A stand-in for a real wind and field model (fudge register).

params.description: equator's rate, degrees a day (Snodgrass and Ulrich 1990: 14.713); only the ratios matter
sin² term, degrees a day (−2.396)
sin⁴ term, degrees a day (−1.787)

references: Snodgrass, H. B. and Ulrich, R. K. 1990, Rotation of Doppler features in the solar photosphere, ApJ 351, 309: ω = A + B sin²φ + C sin⁴φ with A = 14.713, B = −2.396, C = −1.787 degrees a day. doi:10.1086/168467
atoms.shown: ω(φ)/ω_eq = (A + B sin²φ + C sin⁴φ) / A

equation.name: How fast a star's surface turns at a latitude, as a share of its equator's rate
equation.formula:
s2 = sin(phi) * sin(phi)
w = (A + B * s2 + C * s2 * s2) / A

source.text: Snodgrass, H. B. and Ulrich, R. K. 1990, ApJ 351, 309

explain.curious: A star is not solid: its equator goes round faster than its poles. On the Sun the equator laps the poles about every three months, which drags spots and filaments into slanting streaks.
explain.science: The Sun's surface rate from Doppler features, used for every cool star scaled to its own equator's spin (a stand-in: Barnes et al. 2005 find the shear depends weakly on temperature). Unverified until the paper search returns.

params.description: mean latitude of new spot groups as a cycle begins, degrees (Hathaway 2015: about 25 to 30)
mean latitude at the cycle's end, degrees (about 8)

references: Hathaway, D. H. 2015, The solar cycle, Living Reviews in Solar Physics 12, 4: spot groups appear near 25 to 30 degrees latitude early in a cycle and drift toward about 8 degrees by its end (Spörer's law, the butterfly diagram); groups follow Joy's law and Hale's polarity law. https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.07020
atoms.shown: φ = L0 − (L0 − L1) ψ, ψ the share of the cycle gone since its minimum

equation.name: Where on a star new spot groups appear as its cycle goes on

psi.name: share of the cycle gone since its minimum

L0.name: latitude as a cycle begins, degrees

phi.name: mean latitude of new spot groups

source.text: Hathaway, D. H. 2015, Living Reviews in Solar Physics 12, 4

explain.curious: Early in each cycle the Sun's spots break out at mid latitudes; as the cycle goes on they appear nearer and nearer the equator. Plotted against time they make the famous butterfly wings.
explain.science: A straight line through the cycle as a stand-in for the measured curve (fudge register), with a spread drawn about it. Used for every star with a cycle; stars without one place their spots by a separate stand-in. Unverified until the paper search returns.

params.description: tilt at the pole, degrees (Stenflo and Kosovichev 2012: 32.1)

references: Stenflo, J. O. and Kosovichev, A. G. 2012, Bipolar magnetic regions on the Sun: global analysis of the SOHO/MDI data set, ApJ 745, 129: tilt angle γ ≈ 32.1° sin φ (Joy's law). https://arxiv.org/abs/1112.5226

Hathaway, D. H. 2015, The solar cycle, Living Reviews in Solar Physics 12, 4: spot groups appear near 25 to 30 degrees latitude early in a cycle and drift toward about 8 degrees by its end (Spörer's law, the butterfly diagram); groups follow Joy's law and Hale's polarity law. https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.07020
atoms.shown: γ = 32.1° sin|φ|, the leading spot nearer the equator

equation.name: How far a spot group's pair is tilted from east to west

gamma.name: tilt of the pair, leading spot toward the equator

source.text: Stenflo, J. O. and Kosovichev, A. G. 2012, ApJ 745, 129

explain.curious: Spots come in pairs of opposite magnetic sign. The leading one sits a little nearer the equator, and more so the further from the equator the pair is: the twist the star's spin gives the rising field.
explain.science: Joy's law from magnetograms of the Sun, used for every star with spots (a stand-in for other stars). Unverified until the paper search returns.

params.description: decay rate, millionths of a hemisphere a day (Petrovay and van Driel-Gesztelyi 1997: about 10)

references: Petrovay, K. and van Driel-Gesztelyi, L. 1997, Making sense of sunspot decay. I. Parabolic decay law and Gnevyshev-Waldmeier relation, Solar Physics 176, 249: a group's lifetime is about its peak area over W ≈ 10 millionths of a hemisphere a day. doi:10.1023/A:1004988123265
atoms.shown: T = A / W, W ≈ 10 millionths of a hemisphere a day

equation.name: How long a spot group lives for its size

A.name: a spot group's peak area, millionths of a hemisphere

W.name: decay rate, millionths of a hemisphere a day

source.text: Petrovay, K. and van Driel-Gesztelyi, L. 1997, Solar Physics 176, 249

explain.curious: Big spots last longer: a small spot is gone in a few days, a huge group can last for months.
explain.science: The Gnevyshev-Waldmeier rule: spots shrink at a steady rate in area, so life is peak area over that rate. Used for every star's spot groups (a stand-in for other stars). Unverified until the paper search returns.
